User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Pacific Software: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 5 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Schwab. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have the receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Thanks — I can walk through what’s deductible, whether you should itemize, how to treat the home office, and which IRS forms you’ll need. A couple of quick clarifying questions before I run any dollar-by-dollar estimates:
- Is the $3,200 of student-loan interest the amount you actually paid in tax year 2024 (not an aggregate from prior years)? The student-loan interest deduction only applies to interest paid during the tax year.
- Are the $540 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses related to your freelance writing (e.g., supplies, software, travel), or are they unreimbursed employee expenses from a W-2 job? (Employee unreimbursed expenses are generally not deductible for 2018–2025 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.)

Summary (high level)
- Report all income: W-2 wages, freelance income, and interest/dividends (Capital One and Schwab) on your Form 1040.
- Freelance income (the $18,400) is reported on Schedule C. Ordinary and necessary business expenses for that freelance work reduce your Schedule C net profit.
- Self-employment tax (Social Security + Medicare) applies to your Schedule C net profit; you calculate it on Schedule SE. You can deduct half of the self-employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1.
- Home office: you can claim a home-office deduction for your freelance work either by the simplified method or the actual method. You can still take the standard deduction on your Form 1040 and also claim the home-office deduction on Schedule C — the home-office deduction is not an “itemized” deduction.
- Student loan interest is an above-the-line adjustment (Schedule 1) up to a limit (generally $2,500) but phases out at higher incomes — whether you qualify depends on your MAGI.
- Charitable giving ($1,500) is deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). There is no general above-the-line deduction for cash gifts for most taxpayers for tax years after the temporary pandemic rules.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses are generally nondeductible; business unreimbursed expenses are deductible on Schedule C.

Home office — your options and quick math
You stated: home office 120 sq ft exclusive; total home 720 sq ft → business use percentage = 120 / 720 = 16.6667% (≈16.67%).

- Simplified method: IRS allows $5 per square foot up to 300 sq ft. That gives 120 × $5 = $600 deduction on Schedule C.
- Actual method (since you rent): you can deduct the business portion of your rent and other indirect home expenses. Example using rent only: $1,750 × 12 = $21,000 rent × 16.67% = $3,500 business-share of rent. That is substantially larger than the simplified-method amount. If you have utilities, renter’s insurance, or other shared home expenses, their business shares could be deductible as well under the actual method. For actual-method calculations you generally use Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) and transfer the allowed deduction to Schedule C.
- Important constraint: the home-office deduction cannot exceed your net profit from that business. Based on the numbers you gave (18,400 freelance minus $540 expenses = $17,860 pre-home-office profit), a $3,500 home-office deduction is allowable because it’s less than that profit. Any disallowed amount (if it exceeded profit) may carry forward.

Student loan interest
- The student-loan interest deduction is an adjustment to income (Schedule 1) of up to $2,500 in most cases. The deduction phases out as your MAGI rises (phaseout thresholds apply for single filers).
- If the $3,200 is interest you actually paid in 2024, the maximum deductible amount is typically $2,500, but you may be ineligible or partially phased out depending on your MAGI. Your tentative gross income before adjustments (W-2 + freelance + interest) is about $117,420, which likely puts you at or above many phaseout thresholds — so you may not be able to claim the student-loan interest deduction in full (or at all). I can check the exact phaseout determination if you want me to run the numbers.

Charitable gifts and itemizing
- You have $1,500 of charitable cash contributions (receipt available). That is deductible only if you itemize on Schedule A.
- Other typical itemizable items (mortgage interest, state and local taxes, large medical expenses, etc.) were not listed, so with only $1,500 in charitable gifts, your total itemized deductions will almost certainly be less than the standard deduction for a single filer. That means you’ll likely take the standard deduction.
- Important: taking the standard deduction does not prevent you from claiming the home-office deduction (that is taken on Schedule C).

Unreimbursed expenses
- If the $540 are business expenses for your freelance activity, deduct them on Schedule C (they reduce self-employment net profit).
- If they are unreimbursed employee expenses from your W-2 job, they are not deductible for federal tax (through 2025, under TCJA), except in very limited categories.

Self-employment tax and QBI
- You’ll owe self-employment tax on the freelance net profit (calculated on Schedule SE). Half of the self-employment tax is deductible as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1).
- You may also be eligible for the Qualified Business Income (QBI) 20% deduction (Form 8995 or 8995-A) on up to 20% of your qualified business income from the Schedule C activity, subject to rules and thresholds. With the income levels you reported you are likely under the high-income phase-in thresholds for QBI, so you may be able to claim a QBI deduction. It’s worth calculating — it can be a sizable additional deduction.

Which forms you’ll likely need
- Form 1040 (main income tax return)
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments to Income) — for adjustments such as half of SE tax and student loan interest (if allowable)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report freelance writing income and business expenses
- Schedule SE (Self-Employment Tax) — to compute SE tax
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you choose the actual method for the home office (not needed if you use the simplified method)
- Form 8995 or 8995-A — to claim the Qualified Business Income deduction (8995 for the simple calculation if you’re under the threshold; 8995-A for the more complex computation)
- Schedule A (Itemized Deductions) — only if you decide to itemize (to deduct the $1,500 charity); otherwise you will take the standard deduction
- Schedule B — if your interest/dividend income requires reporting (usually only if you exceed certain thresholds or have many payers; small amounts can be reported on Schedule 1 lines)

Other practical items and tips
- Make sure you have 1099-NEC / 1099-MISC forms (if any) from your clients; even if you didn’t receive a 1099, you must report the income.
- Make sure you have 1099-INT (Capital One) or 1099-DIV (Schwab) for your interest/dividends and report those amounts on Form 1040.
- Because you have freelance income, you may need to pay quarterly estimated taxes (federal) to avoid penalties.
- Keep receipts supporting your business expenses and the home-office calculation (square footage, rent, utilities if deducting them).
- For student loan interest you should have Form 1098-E from your loan servicer showing interest paid in the tax year.

Bottom-line recommendations
- It’s almost certainly better to take the standard deduction (you have only $1,500 of charitable donations and no other listed itemized items), but you can still claim the home-office deduction on Schedule C.
- Use the actual home-office method (Form 8829) if your business-share of rent and other indirect expenses (utilities, renter’s insurance) is large — based on rent alone, actual-method rent share of ~ $3,500 > simplified-method $600.
- Confirm whether the $540 are Schedule C expenses — if so, deduct them on Schedule C.
- Confirm whether the $3,200 student loan interest is interest paid in 2024; if yes, up to $2,500 may be deductible but you may be phased out given your income. I can run the phaseout calculation for you.

Would you like me to:
- Run a rough worksheet showing your taxable income and estimated federal tax under (a) simplified home-office and (b) actual home-office and (c) standard vs itemized, using the numbers you provided? If so, please confirm whether the $3,200 student loan interest is for 2024 and whether the $540 is freelance business expense.
